The vote follows a lawsuit filed in September by former student Jane Doe alleging sexual assault and forced drug use at the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, which sparked protests and scrutiny of the university's response policies.
Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the resolution, said last week that "the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg," while 165 faculty members supported the measure.

Although the Faculty Senate lacks dismissal authority, Board of Trustees chair Anne Meinig Smalling confirmed the board remains confident in Kotlikoff's leadership, despite acknowledging campus distress from the vote.

The university awaits an independent review led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, while New York Attorney General Letitia James oversees a separate criminal investigation into the 2024 allegations.

Eisenberg led the division handling espionage, terrorism, and leak investigations, including the high-profile prosecution of former National Security Adviser John Bolton over classified material retention.

Quiñones had been overseeing high-profile matters out of South Florida, including prosecutions targeting foreign leaders like former Cuban President Raúl Castro and inquiries involving former CIA Director John Brennan.
Their resignations immediately follow the departure of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who stepped down as head of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division on Thursday.

Tech executives and billionaires donated more than $333 million to the nonprofit Building a Better California to oppose the measure. California Gov. Gavin Newsom also opposed it, criticizing the plan for directing "almost all of the revenue" to healthcare.

Election results revealed regional divides across California, with wealthy Bay Area enclaves Marin County and San Mateo County voting against Prop 40. However, 55% of San Francisco County voters favored the measure, reflecting a stark geographic split.

Opponents simultaneously promoted competing ballot measures designed to nullify wealth taxes , with Prop 42 leading in early vote tallies. That measure would prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets, and retirement holdings.

Michael Feispor, partner on EY's private tax team, stated a "no" vote doesn't mean similar measures won't return. Wealthy Californians are already revisiting residency and estate planning structures to prepare for future wealth tax proposals.

summary: On Thursday, Novartis disclosed nine reports of tumors in patients treated with Zolgensma, its spinal muscular atrophy gene therapy, with two cases showing evidence that the virus used for delivery integrated into patient DNA .

Zolgensma, developed by AveXis, treats SMA by packaging a gene into an AAV to stimulate SMN protein production; researchers have long feared AAVs could potentially integrate into human DNA, a risk listed in therapy warnings.

Nine reports of tumors have emerged since Zolgensma's 2019 approval, with seven cases identified recently. Cure SMA noted that three of those patients underwent testing, with one case appearing unrelated to the therapy.

SMA Europe called the reports "deeply concerning for families," urging Novartis to provide clear information rather than leaving patients to piece together safety concerns from social media and incomplete reports.

Regulatory authorities are now examining the cases, as the FDA previously called for greater monitoring of gene therapies following concerns involving UniQure; Novartis said it will continue working with regulators on next steps.
title: FDA probes tumour risk tied to Novartis gene therapy

The Busan agreement, unveiled at an October 2025 summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, required China to increase soybean purchases and roll back export controls on rare earths essential to U.S. industries.

Tensions persist regarding Trump's trade policies, defense spending, and opposition to the International Criminal Court. The European Union is considering a "blocking statute" to protect its institutions from United States secondary sanctions, a move the administration labels hostile.

summary: On Friday, the United States Treasury Department imposed sanctions on eight Canadian money services firms, alleging they facilitated transactions for sanctioned Iranian entities and coordinating with Canadian financial authorities.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated Canada 'cannot be a safe haven' for sanctions evasion, as the Office of Foreign Assets Control alleges firms exchanged Iranian rials into digital assets linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Several sanctioned entities also allegedly laundered millions in drug proceeds for Ryan Wedding, the former Canadian Olympic snowboarder arrested in January. The Drug Enforcement Administration participated in the investigation targeting businesses in Ontario and British Columbia.

These measures effectively cut the firms off from the dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets subject to United States jurisdiction. US persons are prohibited from conducting transactions with designated businesses including Million Exchange and Darvish Exchange.
title: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
US approves potential $1.08 billion Black Hawk helicopter sale to Mexico

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the White House’s shift as an “attempt to rebrand,” stressing political and legal “opposition” to Trump’s proposed arch; the right-leaning account de-emphasizes those disputes and foregrounds the ceremonial title “Military Triumphal Arch,” emphasizing martial symbolism.
Center coverage adds procedural context: the 250-foot structure, new depictions unveiled after a judge paused construction, and mounting resistance.
Thus, the pivotal divide is whether the change represents image management or an honorific military presentation.
Across perspectives, the project’s association with Trump and its military framing remain prominent, revealing contrasting interpretations of political symbolism and public presentation.
summary: On Friday, a U.S. judge paused construction on President Donald Trump's 250-foot arch in Washington, prompting the White House to rebrand the project as the Military Triumphal Arch emphasizing military heritage.

The National Capital Planning Commission voted on Thursday to approve the arch project after hearing from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers, despite concerns near Arlington National Cemetery.

Attorneys general from Virginia and the District of Columbia sued to prevent construction, citing safety concerns near Reagan Washington National Airport and damage to the capital skyline; Trump previously described the structure as a "military complex."
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order on construction, prompting White House spokesman Davis Ingle to criticize the ruling as coming from "an activist district court."

The administration contends Congress authorized the arch over 100 years ago amid Republican Party losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, as new renderings showcase a "GOLDEN AGE OF AMERICA" theme and the United States Triumphal Arch Foundation claims independence.
title: White House recasts Trump arch as military tribute

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes Microsoft ’s reassessment of more than $80 billion in cloud contracts, using “switching off” to stress the scale of change, while right-leaning coverage uses “pulls the plug” and “fallout” to portray abrupt termination and post-election data-center disruption.

Center coverage adds technical context: older Nvidia chips reportedly failed to meet requirements, Microsoft may favor its own facilities and fewer neocloud partners, and Oracle shares fell nearly 3%.

The perspectives agree Microsoft did not renew the Oracle arrangement amid a broader cloud-strategy review, but differ over whether it signals routine recalibration, infrastructure strain, or wider investment consequences.
summary: On Friday, Microsoft began winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle as part of a broader reassessment of more than $80 billion in cloud partnerships, Bloomberg News reported.

Initiated in 2023 to support Microsoft's AI-powered Bing search engine, the contract involved older Nvidia chips that no longer met the company's evolving technical specifications, according to the report.
Oracle resold the capacity at a 20% premium to other customers under long-term contracts, with most GPUs covered by these renewals at least four years old, the company said.

In afternoon trading, Oracle shares fell nearly 3% while Microsoft stock remained little changed, though the cloud provider maintains its existing hardware continues attracting significant customer interest.
To address high costs and delays, Microsoft is increasing oversight of data center construction by sending employees to supplier sites, affecting partnerships with Nscale and Nebius.
title: Microsoft Is Winding Down Oracle Deal to Rent AI Cloud Capacity, Reports Say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the withdrawal as a political and legal defeat—“waves white flag,” “smackdown,” and “massive admission of defeat”—emphasizing risks to lawful voters and an allegedly weak list.

Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds election integrity, “20,000” suspected noncitizen ballots, Supreme Court rejection, and the DOJ’s claim that ballots would be commingled, while “about-face” casts the retreat skeptically; it also highlights the possibility of legitimate concerns.
Center coverage de-emphasizes partisan triumph, stressing procedural impracticality and an outdated list.
All acknowledge the dismissal and disputed ballots, but their divide reflects wider conflict over voter security, federal power, and election legitimacy.
summary: The U.S. Department of Justice moved on Friday to dismiss its lawsuit seeking to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens, citing the impossibility of separating them after processing.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, appointed by former President Bill Clinton, previously denied the government's request to separate ballots, warning that intervening at that late stage would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.
California officials have processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted from the state's 23 million registered voters.

Federal prosecutor Bill Essayli previously argued the lawsuit was necessary to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election," while state prosecutors arrested over 30 noncitizens accused of illegally registering to vote.

The Trump administration continues appealing the earlier ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, as part of broader efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
title: US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as an arrest based on allegations, emphasizing “allegedly,” the suspect’s claim that he “heard voices,” and reported weapons without declaring an assassination plot; right-leaning coverage portrays authorities as thwarting an “assassination threat,” foregrounding “armed Venezuelan migrant,” “illegal alien,” “Biden-Released,” “busted,” and a “small arsenal” to connect the incident to border policy and Democratic responsibility.

Center coverage more consistently preserves uncertainty about intent through phrases such as “DHS says” and “alleged.” All perspectives stress the arrest, stolen vehicle, and firearms, revealing a shared concern over security but a broader divide over immigration, mental illness, and political accountability.
summary: On Thursday, Secret Service officers arrested Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos on Constitution Avenue near the White House after discovering three firearms in a stolen vehicle; Chrinos allegedly claimed voices told him to kill President Donald Trump .

Records show Chrinos entered the U.S. illegally via Texas in March 2024 under the catch-and-release policy, prompting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to lodge a detainer against the Venezuelan national following his arrest.
Authorities discovered an AR-15-style rifle and two handguns in the vehicle, and Chrinos remains in U.S. Marshals Service custody facing multiple weapons and theft charges.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised the Secret Service for de-escalating a situation that "posed an imminent threat to our protectees," while the White House deferred comment to the Department of Homeland Security.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran expressed being "alarmed by the increase in threat cases," noting this arrest reflects a persistent pattern of armed individuals drawn to the White House complex since Trump returned to office.
title: Secret Service arrests man near White House after he said he heard voices telling him to kill Trump
Democrat Nancy Lacore wins election to U.S. House in South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Gaza ’s flooding as an urgent accountability crisis, stressing “displaced” families, “drowning” camps, “immediate intervention,” and 1,500 distress calls while declaring that “the occupation bears responsibility.” Right-leaning coverage likewise emphasizes “refugee tents,” “widespread destruction,” and even “genocidal war,” but foregrounds Civil Defence accounts and visual or eyewitness references rather than the rights group’s appeal.
Center coverage de-emphasizes blame, presenting rain, collapsed walls, and “worsening hardship” in restrained humanitarian terms.

The pivotal divide is whether prior Israeli damage is contextual background or the cause of today’s suffering; all perspectives nonetheless emphasize flooding, two wounded Palestinians, and the broader vulnerability produced by war and displacement.
summary: On Saturday, November 7, heavy rainfall flooded thousands of displacement tents across the Gaza Strip, while a wall collapsed in northern Gaza, injuring two people near Nuseirat and Gaza City.

Gaza's emergency committee reports more than one million displaced people face winter dangers, with the territory urgently needing about 200,000 tents and heating supplies to protect families in worn-out shelters.
Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told Al Jazeera that crews received about 1,500 distress calls in 10 hours as water levels rose 30-40 cm. "What we feared has actually happened," Basal said.

Aid groups blame Israeli restrictions on shelter materials for hampering response efforts; Mohammed Salha, director of the Palestinian NGO Network, noted 50,000 tents remain waiting on the Egyptian side of the border.

In southern Gaza, more than 900,000 displaced people sheltering in al-Mawasi face ongoing risks, while more than 125,000 families along the coast remain at particular risk of having their tents swept away by the sea.
title: Two Palestinians Wounded as Rain Causes Collapse of Wall in Israeli-Damaged Building in Gaza

bias: Coverage converges on Abdul El-Sayed ’s opposition to U.S. support for Israel and willingness to work with Trump, but diverges in emphasis: left-leaning framing highlights his “praises” of a reported $4 billion cut and cross-party cooperation; center coverage presents “rare common ground” while adding his broader call to end aid and ban weapons sales, plus his distinction between Judaism and Israel; right-leaning framing foregrounds “subsidize a foreign military,” “awful things,” and weapons allegedly used harmfully.
The pivotal divide is whether this is pragmatic cooperation, expanded policy, or moral condemnation—though all stress reducing U.S. military support.
summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced plans to end approximately $4 billion in annual United States military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, citing an earlier agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed welcomed the decision during an appearance on Thursday's Morning Joe, stating, "I think the president is actually right on this policy."

El-Sayed, the first Muslim American elected to the Senate, called for halting American arms sales to Israel, arguing taxpayer dollars should not fund actions he described as "genocide" and "apartheid" in Gaza and the West Bank.

The Democrat rejected claims that criticizing Israel constitutes antisemitism, emphasizing the need to separate Judaism from Israeli government policies while affirming commitment to Jewish children's safety.
El-Sayed advocated for a broader review of military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Pakistan, arguing American taxpayer dollars should be prioritized for domestic needs instead.
title: El-Sayed backs Trump plan to end Israel aid: ‘I agree with him on that’

summary: On Monday, the Crown withdrew all criminal charges against 44 pro-Palestinian protesters arrested during an April 2024 sit-in at a downtown Montreal Scotiabank, officially ending the prosecution.
Protesters occupied the branch demanding Scotiabank divest from Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, a move the bank eventually completed, which activists welcomed as a victory.

While 14 individuals previously pleaded guilty to municipal noise bylaw violations and paid $300 fines, defense lawyer Barbara Bedont noted most other protesters resolved their cases through community service.
Defendants challenged the charges under the Charter, arguing police violated their rights, and filed a formal complaint against the presiding judge alleging bias and unfair treatment.
Defense counsel Bedont warned that criminalizing peaceful sit-ins threatens the right to protest, suggesting the group's legal strategy likely influenced the Crown's decision to drop charges.
title: No Criminal Charges for Montreal Protesters Arrested at Bank Sit-In

During a Wednesday monologue, Kimmel accused Trump of dividing the country and urged him to resign.

bias: Left- and right-leaning coverage largely converges, framing SpaceXAI’s construction as allegedly “without necessary permits” and potentially “violating state water pollution laws,” with fines up to $6.1 million.

The left emphasizes environmental and corporate accountability, while the right’s similar focus on compliance and enforcement resonates with law-and-order concerns; neither uses strongly partisan terms such as “woke” or “far-left.” The pivotal dividing line is whether “alleges” preserves uncertainty or whether “violating” implies culpability.

Center coverage adds investor disclosure and the possibility fines could “exceed $6M.” All emphasize regulatory scrutiny and financial consequences, reflecting shared concern over development versus oversight.
summary: Environmental regulators released details this week on penalties against SpaceXAI for violating Mississippi water pollution laws by starting construction on its Southaven data center facilities without required permits.

During a July meeting, officials discovered MZX Tech LLC had already begun construction on approximately 30 acres, prompting the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality to issue violation notices on August 10.

Inspectors at the 2400 Stateline Road property found "no steps have been taken to protect stormwater infrastructure at the site," which neighbors Horn Lake Creek, risking chemical runoff into local waters.
Separately, U.S. District Court Judge Debra Brown ruled last week that MDEQ misinterpreted Clean Air Act statutes when allowing SpaceXAI to run 69 natural gas turbines without a permit.

SpaceXAI informed investors two weeks ago that potential fines could reach $6.1 million, and the Elon Musk-owned company stated in an October filing it is cooperating with the agency to resolve matters through an agreed order.
title: SpaceXAI started Southaven data center construction without water permits, Mississippi alleges
